key_concept: Cell theory was formulated by Matthias Schleiden (1838, plants) and Theodor Schwann (1839, animals), and Rudolf Virchow (1855) later modified it.
steps: In 1838, the German botanist Matthias Schleiden studied many plants and concluded that all plants are made of different kinds of cells that form the tissues of the plant.

In 1839, the British zoologist Theodor Schwann studied animal cells. He noted that cells have a thin outer layer, now called the plasma membrane, and that plant cells also have a cell wall. He proposed that the bodies of animals and plants are made of cells and their products.
Together, these ideas form the cell theory, so it is credited to Schleiden and Schwann.

Their theory did not explain how new cells form. In 1855, Rudolf Virchow added that new cells arise only from pre-existing cells ($\textit{Omnis cellula-e cellula}$), which gave the modern form of cell theory.
Match with the options: only Option (1) names the formulators, which agrees with the NTA key.
why_not_others: Robert Brown discovered the nucleus, Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane (1972), and Leeuwenhoek was the first to see and describe a live cell. None of them formulated cell theory.
common_trap: Students confuse 'first to see a live cell' (Leeuwenhoek) or 'modified cell theory' (Virchow) with 'formulated cell theory' (Schleiden and Schwann).
time_saving_tip: Memorise the scientist–discovery pairs: Leeuwenhoek → live cell, Brown → nucleus, Schleiden and Schwann → cell theory, Virchow → $\textit{Omnis cellula-e cellula}$, Singer and Nicolson → fluid mosaic model.
